entries.title: Setup assembles shared supplies, personal boards, and starting hands
entries.summary: Make the goods, ships, special tiles, building tiles, mountain strips, occupation cards, and weapon cards available as directed. Each player receives a home board, their Vikings, a starting occupation card, the specified starter weapons, and a starter food tile; choose the long or short home-board side before play. Keep all personal goods and cards visible, while exact component sorting and starting-card identity remain tied to the selected document and printing.

entries.title: The strategic target is valuable, well-covered personal boards
entries.summary: Build value by acquiring goods, ships, houses, exploration boards, animals, and occupations, then arranging goods on the home and added boards. Coverage matters twice: it can expose income and bonuses during play while also reducing negative spaces for final scoring. Treat the placement geometry as a planning system, not merely storage.

entries.title: Rounds follow a fixed twelve-phase sequence
entries.summary: For the multiplayer game described here, resolve in order: add a Viking, harvest, update exploration boards and silver, draw a weapon, place Vikings for actions, determine the next start player, collect income, breed animals, hold the feast, collect bonuses, update mountain strips, and return placed Vikings. The document describes a six-round short game and a seven-round long game; do not silently apply this sequence to solo or expansion rules.

entries.title: The action phase is contested worker placement
entries.summary: Starting with the current start player and proceeding clockwise, place one or more available Vikings on one unoccupied action space and resolve at least one effect immediately. Continue until each player has passed or placed all available Vikings. A player who passes cannot place again that round, and an action space cannot be occupied twice in the same round.

entries.title: Action-space column controls the Viking commitment
entries.summary: The action board's columns require different numbers of Vikings: the first column uses one, then later columns use two, three, or four. The required Vikings are a placement cost, not a promise that every depicted effect is optional; occupy a space only when you can use at least one effect and pay any required cost. Read the selected action space for its exact production, exchange, ship, expedition, occupation, or risk procedure.

source_locator.locator: Phase 5: Actions; The Action Spaces; pp. 9, 14–21

entries.title: Cards are visible tactical inventory, not a hidden hand
entries.summary: Starting occupations, drawn weapons, and later occupation cards are kept face up and visible. The action board and occupation actions determine when a card can enter play, while card effects can be immediate or available at any time according to their presentation. Do not infer an occupation or weapon's exact cost, timing, or value from its title; consult the exact component or an authorized current reference.

entries.title: Anytime placement converts inventory into an irreversible board plan
entries.summary: Goods, silver, and ore can be placed on eligible home, exploration, or house spaces outside the main action placement, subject to each board's adjacency and covered-space rules. Ships can be bought with silver, and ships may be armed with ore. Once a tile or ore is committed to a board or ship it cannot be taken back, so test layouts before committing and preserve feast or income needs when upgrading goods.

entries.title: Most exchanges advance goods through a constrained value ladder
entries.summary: Production, mountain actions, crafting, trading, overseas trading, ship use, exploration, and emigration are distinct action families. The general exchange pattern upgrades goods along their color/value path while respecting the selected action's quantity, shape, ship, or payment limits; a knarr gates overseas trading. Use the printed action space for the exact exchange and never treat an upgrade as permission to ignore feast, placement, or component limits.

source_locator.document_section: Exchange Spaces; Mountain and Trading Actions; Knarr Action Spaces
source_locator.locator: Exchange Spaces; Mountain and Trading Actions; Knarr Action Spaces; pp. 15–16

entries.title: The feast is a recurring food-placement check
entries.summary: During the feast phase, fill empty banquet spaces with eligible food tiles or one-silver coins while respecting the board's adjacency and fit rules. Orange and red food have their own spacing restrictions, and ore is not a feast substitute. Every unfilled space produces a Thing Penalty tile that remains through the game and reduces final value, so income and food planning should be assessed before converting supplies.

entries.title: Income, breeding, and bonuses are separate maintenance windows
entries.summary: After actions, determine start-player order, collect silver from the lowest currently uncovered income value, resolve animal breeding in the animal spaces, then collect goods bonuses whose surrounding spaces have been covered. This separation matters: income is silver, breeding changes animal supply, and bonuses are goods; do not merge them into one generic production step.

entries.title: Final value combines assets, coverage, penalties, and occupations
entries.summary: After the selected six- or seven-round game ends, evaluate the value of ships, houses, exploration boards, and placed goods, account for animals and occupations, and apply negative spaces and Thing Penalty tiles. The winner is the player with the greatest resulting value. Exact tile values, occupation values, and board-specific scoring must be read from the current components and are not reproduced here.
